images.filename: Fossil trail of giant myriapod - geograph.org.uk - 854033.jpg
images.caption:
Fossil trail of giant myriapod of the family Arthropleuridae near Laggan, Isle of Arran, Scotland. Two parallel fossil tracks running down and left from the pointing fingers. These are on a sloping slab of Carboniferous sandstone (about 300 Million years old) on the RH side of a narrow shingly inlet close to the “Duchess Anne’s salt pan” building.[1] For discussion of arthropleurid trace fossils (this one belongs to the ichnogenus Diplichnites), see Briggs et al. (1979).[2]
Not visible, by the camera position, there is a 9in. coal seam outcropping. These local coal exposures provided the incentive to evaporate sea water for its salt in the salt pans (from 1710 to 1735).[1]
images.alt:

images.filename: Flame structure at Lochranza harbour - geograph.org.uk - 1158903.jpg
images.caption:
Flame structure at Lochranza harbour On a very rocky beach next to the ferry port there is a rock. Just above the pencil (a scale) you can see a chalk outline. This is a flame structure. 
They form when sediment is put on top of another sediment and some goes into the other sediment. Eg. when you tread on sand the sand goes through your toes. 

This is a 'way up' structure as it tells you what way the sediments were originally. Another example of a way up structure is a tree stump. If you find it upside down then you know the beds have been over turned.

images.caption: Sannox 'sheep' This iron sheep is firmly fixed to the end of the jetty at Sannox and is used as a mooring bollard. Perhaps it should be a bull with a ring through its nose, then it could be called a 'moo-ring' bollard.  Similar sheep feature at Corrie; all four harbours on this section of coast are looked after by the Corrie and Sannox Harbour Trust.

images.caption:
Circle 4 at Machrie Moor.
Four rounded granite blocks, just less than 1m high. In the middle distance on the left is the large stone of circle 3 and on the right are the three large stones of circle 2. In the far distance are the mountains of the north of Arran, consisting of Beinn Tarsuinn and Goat Fell.
